Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 99, verse 1:

(p-188) Surat al-Zalzala (The Earthquake)

Medinan, with disagreement about it; its verses are eight.

﴿When the earth is shaken﴾ i.e., it is moved with a violent, repeated, successive shaking; that is, the particular quaking pertaining to it according to the will that is founded upon consummate wisdoms, which is the severe quaking beyond which there is no further extent, or its wondrous quaking whose measure cannot be estimated, or its quaking that falls within the realm of possibility. It has been read with a fatha on the zay (al-Zalzal), and it is a noun (ism); there is no pattern fa'lal with a fatha except in doubled (mudaaaf) forms, and the phrase "naqatun khaz'al" (a she-camel that is tall/strong) is rare. It has also been said that "al-zalzal" with a fatha is likewise a verbal noun (masdar), like al-waswas, al-jarjar and al-qalqal; and that occurs at the second blast (al-nafkha al-thaniya), according to His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: *

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 99, verse 2:

﴿And the earth brings forth its burdens﴾. That is: what is in its interior of the dead and the hidden treasures. "Athqal" (burdens) is the plural of "thiql," which is the household goods (mata' al-bayt). The mention of "the earth" (al-ard) in the place where a pronoun would be expected is for the sake of greater emphasis (li-ziyadat al-taqrir), or as an allusion (li-l-iima') to the earth being changed into another earth (tubaddul al-ard ghayr al-ard), or because the bringing forth of the burdens is the state of some of its parts (li-anna ikhraj al-athqal hal ba'd ajza'iha).

"And man will say," that is, every individual among mankind, at what overwhelms them of the complete catastrophe and what dazzles them of the all-encompassing calamity, "What is wrong with it?" — meaning, the earth has been shaken with this severe degree of quaking and has brought forth its burdens, in awe of what they have witnessed of the tremendous matter, and the mountains have been set moving through the air and turned into scattered dust. It was also said: this is the statement of the disbeliever when he does not believe in the Resurrection. The more apparent view, however, is the first, on the basis that the believer says it by way of extolling (the magnitude of the event), while the disbeliever says it by way of amazement.

"﴿Yawma'idhin﴾" is a substitute (badal) for "idha", and His statement, exalted is He, ﴿tuhaddithu akhbaraha﴾ ("it will relate its news") governs both of them. It is also permissible for "idha" to be in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: on the day when the earth is shaken, it will inform the creation of its news, either by the tongue of its state, in that it clearly indicates what its quaking and the bringing forth of its burdens are for, or by the tongue of speech, in that God, exalted is He, causes it to speak, so it informs of what good and evil was done upon it. And it has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it bears witness over every person to what he did upon its back. (p-189) It has also been read as "tunbi akhbaraha" ("it will report its news"), and it has been read as "min al-inba'" (from the reporting).

﴿Bi-anna rabbaka awha lahā﴾ (﴿That your Lord had inspired her﴾). That is: she relates her news because your Lord inspired her to do so and commanded her to relate it, according to one of the two interpretations. It is also permissible for this to be a substitute (badal) for "her news," as if it were said: she relates her news, [namely] that your Lord had inspired [her]; because the verb tuhaddithu (to relate) is used both with the preposition bi (bi-) and without it. And "awha lahā" (inspired her) carries the meaning of "awha ilayhā" (inspired to her).

**﴿On that Day﴾**, i.e., the day when what has been mentioned takes place, **﴿people will issue forth﴾** from their graves toward the place of reckoning (*mawqif al-hisab*), **﴿in scattered groups﴾**, dispersed according to their classes (*tabaqat*): white-faced and secure, and black-faced and terrified, as has passed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you will come in throngs﴾. It has also been said: they will issue forth from the place of standing in scattered groups, some to the right toward Paradise and some to the left toward the Fire.

**﴿That they may be shown their deeds﴾**, i.e., the recompense for their deeds, whether good or evil. It is recited as **"liyarawu"** (لِيَرَوْا) with a fatha, meaning the verb is read with the fatha on the final vowel, so that the form is the subjunctive (*nasb*) of the plural verb.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 99, verses 7–8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ ﴿and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ is an elaboration of "they will be shown" (yaraw). It is read "yurahu" as well. The dharrah (atom, or ant) is the small ant; it is said that it is what is seen in the sunlight from the dust motes (haba'). Whichever it is, the meaning of seeing what is equivalent to it of good and evil is either witnessing its recompense, in which case the first "man" (whoever) is specific to the blessed and the second to the wretched. How could it not be so? The good deeds of the disbeliever are nullified by disbelief, and the bad deeds of the believer who avoids the major sins are forgiven. As for what is said, that the good deed of the disbeliever has an effect in lessening the punishment, it is refuted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾. Or it is witnessing the deed itself without taking into account either its recompense or its absence; rather, each of the two is left to the other clear evidences affirming the forgiveness of the minor sins of the believer who avoids the major sins, and his reward for all his good deeds, and the nullification of the good deeds of the disbeliever and his punishment for all his sins. So the meaning is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: there is no believer or disbeliever who does good or evil except that Allah, exalted is He, shows it to him. As for the believer, He forgives him his evil deeds and rewards him for his good deeds; as for the disbeliever, He returns his good deeds to him as regret, and punishes him for his evil deeds.

From the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surat al-Zalzalah four times, it is as if he has recited the entire Qur'an." And Allah knows best.
